chunks: "Bond wires are the tiny wires that connect the pads on the silicon die to the leads or substrate of the package.
They're typically gold, copper or aluminum, around 15 to 50 micrometres in diameter, which is thinner than a human hair.
A machine welds one end to a pad on the die, usually as a ball bond, then arcs the wire over and welds the other end to a lead finger or substrate pad as a stitch or wedge bond.
It does this for every pin, many wires per second. They're popular because they're cheap, flexible, and can connect any die layout to any package without special tooling.
But they're not ideal wires. A few millimetres of wire is about a nanohenry per millimetre of inductance and a few tenths of an ohm of resistance.
At fast edges that inductance matters: L di over dt causes ground bounce and supply droop, and at GHz it limits RF and high-speed I/O.
That's one reason high-performance chips go to flip chip, where the connection is a short solder bump instead.
And since the wire is thin, current capacity is limited, so power pins use several wires in parallel."
